doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Moving to New York in 1950 and Darrow Institute
summary: He followed his future wife north and studied on the G.I. Bill at Darrow Institute, now playing alto with clarinet doubling.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You’re continuing to develop your facility and artistry on your instrument, and you’re getting validation from people like Dizzy Gillespie and the cats in his band...
Yeah.
...and people like Illinois Jacquet...
Jacquet, right.
...and they’re telling you to come to New York—and you spend some time in New York. So finally, in 1950, was it...
Yeah.
You make the move. Talk about the circumstances. I gather that you followed your
future wife, who moved here.

Yes, I followed my future wife. Because she came up as like a work-in maid or whatever it was. You know, they used to get girls from the South, bring them to New York, and they’d work. She came up here, then I said, “Well, I got to go,” and I came on up. I had a good set-up, because I didn’t have to do any work, because I was a G.I. So I went to the Darrow Institute of Music.
On the G.I. Bill?
Yeah, on the G.I. Bill.
Where was Darrow Institute of Music?
58th-59th and Broadway.
What sort of school was it?
You know, a music school. A lot of musicians. Right next to it was the Hartnett Studio, and they had big bands all day, so I could go over and sit in the section and practice.
At this point, you’re playing primarily alto saxophone?
Alto saxophone.
Clarinet is a doubling instrument by now.
Yeah, doubling. I was about to throw that away.
So you’re a full-fledged alto saxophonist.
Yes, alto saxophone.
By the way, what your late wife’s name?
Maker. Maker Donaldson.
